name: Arneis

lines.s10: Arneis is Piedmont's soft, dry white from the Roero hills: ripe pear, camomile and a gentle twist of almond.
lines.s20: Arneis comes from Roero, the sandy hills across the river from Barolo in Piedmont. It is a dry, rounded white of ripe pear, white peach and camomile, soft in acidity, with a faint bitterness of almond on the finish.
lines.s45: Arneis is said to mean little rascal in the dialect of Piedmont, and growers say the vine earns the name. Its home is Roero, the sandy hills across the river Tanaro from Barolo. It tastes of ripe pear, white peach and camomile, with a faint bitterness of almond at the end. It is dry and rounded, medium in body, and soft in acidity. It is made in steel, without oak, and meant to be enjoyed young. Pour it with cured meats, cold veal in tuna sauce or fresh pasta in butter. It once grew among the Nebbiolo vines and softened the red, which earned it the nickname white Barolo.
lines.sale: Arneis is what Piedmont pours before the Barolo: a dry, rounded white of ripe pear and camomile that wakes the appetite without a sharp word. I would start the table with it, beside the cured meats or the veal.

glass.lead: Ripe pear and white peach with camomile and acacia blossom, round and soft, ending on a faint bitter almond.

ladder.where: A hot year or a late harvest in Roero

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium at most and often soft, alcohol moderate, body medium, with a rounded, faintly oily feel.

home.home: Roero, the sandy hills on the left bank of the Tanaro, across the river from Barolo and Barbaresco in Piedmont. Roero Arneis must be at least 95 per cent Arneis. It is made in steel, without oak, to be enjoyed young, and a little is made sparkling. Across the river the same grape is bottled as Langhe Arneis.
home.abroad: It has travelled a little. Australia grows it in Victoria, Tasmania and New South Wales, and Sonoma in California and Oregon's Willamette Valley have some, made in the same fresh, pear scented way.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; too cold and the perfume closes.
service.decant: No. A fresh white with no oak is poured straight from a cold bottle.
service.age: Enjoy it within two or three years; its soft acidity does not favour long keeping.

with.why: the Piedmont match: a soft wine for a creamy sauce
round pear fruit beside salt and fat

with.dish: Fresh egg pasta with butter and sage
with.why: almond and pear sit well with butter
gentle acidity does not fight the cream

labels.means: Arneis, at least 95 per cent, from the Roero hills north of Alba; a DOCG since 2004.
On its own, the zone's red wine, made from Nebbiolo; the white adds the word Arneis.
The same grape from the wider Langhe hills, across the Tanaro from Roero.
A sparkling Roero Arneis, which the same rules allow.

guest.q: I have never heard of Arneis. What is it like?
guest.a: A dry, rounded white from Piedmont, the home of Barolo. Think ripe pear and white peach with a scent of camomile, soft in acidity, and a little almond at the end.
Almost never. It is made in steel to keep its pear and camomile, and its roundness comes from the grape, not from a barrel.

guest.q: The list also shows a Roero with no grape named. Is that the same wine?
guest.a: No. Roero on its own is the red, made from Nebbiolo. The white is labelled Roero Arneis, and it comes from the same sandy hills.

compare.tell: Cortese, as Gavi, is leaner and sharper, with lemon, green apple and high acidity; Arneis is rounder and softer, with ripe pear and almond.
Pinot Blanc is as soft but plainer, with apple and a creamy feel; Arneis is more scented, with ripe pear, camomile and a bitter almond finish.
Vermentino is brisker and saltier, with lime and wild fennel; Arneis is softer and rounder, with ripe pear and camomile.

profile.st: Pale straw · Body medium · Acid medium minus to medium · Alcohol moderate · Dry, round and faintly oily
profile.fruit: Ripe pear, white peach, apricot; green apple from cooler sites and years
profile.other: Camomile, acacia blossom and honeysuckle; a faint bitter almond on the finish; no oak as a rule; honey and hazelnut with a few years
profile.tell: A rounded, softly scented dry white of ripe pear and camomile with gentle acidity and a bitter almond finish: Roero Arneis
profile.regions: Roero and the Langhe in Piedmont; a little in Australia, Sonoma and Oregon's Willamette Valley
profile.confuse: Cortese is leaner and sharper; Pinot Blanc is plainer and less scented; Vermentino is saltier and brisker; Viognier is far more perfumed and fuller

cards.front: Arneis: where is it at home, and what does the label say?
cards.back: Roero, the sandy hills on the left bank of the Tanaro, north of Alba in Piedmont. The wine is Roero Arneis, a DOCG since 2004, at least 95 per cent Arneis.

cards.front: Why was Arneis once nicknamed white Barolo?
cards.back: It was planted among the Nebbiolo vines, and a little was blended into the red to soften it. Nebbiolo Bianco is another of its old names.

cards.front: Arneis blind: what parts it from Cortese, Piedmont's other white?
cards.back: Arneis is rounder and softer, with ripe pear, camomile, bitter almond and gentle acidity. Cortese, as Gavi, is lean and sharp, with lemon and green apple.

questions.q: A list shows two wines side by side, Roero and Roero Arneis. A guest asks how they differ. What do you tell her?
opts: Roero is a red from Nebbiolo; Roero Arneis is the white
Roero is the young wine; Roero Arneis is aged longer
Roero is dry; Roero Arneis is the sweet version
They are one white wine under two names
questions.exp: Roero on its own is the zone's red, made from Nebbiolo. The white carries the grape's name, Roero Arneis. It is no rule of age or of sweetness: both wines are dry.

questions.q: A blind white from Piedmont is dry, round and soft, with gentle acidity: ripe pear, white peach and camomile, a faint bitter almond finish and no oak. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Soft acidity with ripe pear, camomile and bitter almond points to Arneis. Gavi would be leaner and sharper, with lemon and green apple, and Moscato d'Asti is sweet and lightly sparkling.

questions.q: A guest orders cold veal in tuna sauce to begin and asks for a soft, dry white from the dish's own region. Which do you suggest?
questions.exp: Vitello tonnato is a dish of Piedmont, and Roero Arneis is that region's rounded, gentle white. Soave is from the Veneto, Verdicchio from the Marche and Fiano from Campania.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Roero in Piedmont, with Australia, Sonoma and the Willamette Valley given as abroad.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the five targets are Piedmont (whose record already names Arneis), Italy, Australia, the Willamette Valley and Napa and Sonoma, the pages the entry itself supports.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Codex already holds Arneis as Roero's white, pear, camomile, white flowers and almond with soft or moderate acidity and a faint bitterness, rounder than Gavi, for antipasti and vitello tonnato; Roero on the left bank of the Tanaro, sand over marl, DOCG since 2004 for the Nebbiolo red and for Roero Arneis.

The Codex's Piedmont record says the grape was rescued from near extinction in the 1970s. Sources read date the first bottlings of the revival to the 1960s and the low point to the 1970s. The entry leaves the revival out of the spoken line (three grapes of earlier chunks already close on a near loss) and does not contradict the record.
The name: little rascal in Piedmontese is the usual gloss, and the entry gives it as what is said, since the etymology is disputed.

White Barolo and Nebbiolo Bianco, the planting among Nebbiolo and the softening of the red stand on The Oxford Companion to Wine and on the common account; that the two grapes are unrelated is left out, since no source read here states it.

The minimum of 95 per cent Arneis stands on the production rules as the Piedmont region publishes them and on two regional pages; the minimum alcohol (sources give 10.5 and 11 per cent) and the ageing of the Riserva are left out.
Abroad: Victoria, Tasmania and New South Wales, Sonoma and the Willamette Valley stand on two reference pages; Gisborne in New Zealand has one source and is left out.
The ladder is a taster's reading: the grape's acidity is low and it turns soft and honeyed when picked late or in a hot year. No cool rung is given, since no source read describes a cooler home.
No dish from the Creole table is given: the grape's soft acidity suits cream, butter and cured meat better than the spice of that table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
